c.tagline: The Tuareg capital of the Sahara, gateway to the volcanic peaks of the Hoggar mountains

card: Rarely accepted; cash is essential throughout the region

taxi.fareNote: Multi-day Hoggar excursions to Assekrem are typically arranged through a licensed desert guide, not a standard taxi

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 14 for medical/fire emergencies; French is more useful than English with dispatchers

walk: Central Tamanrasset is walkable for markets and the museum; the Hoggar mountains and Assekrem require a 4x4 and licensed guide over several days

safety.safety: Requires advance planning and often a registered guide for excursions outside town; check current travel advisories for southern Algeria before visiting
safety.crime: Low street crime in town; the main risks are desert travel logistics (heat, remoteness) rather than crime

hood_landmark.Town Center: Tamanrasset's central market and Museum of the Hoggar
hood_landmark.Assekrem Plateau (day-trip base): Assekrem's sunrise viewpoint over the Hoggar peaks
hood_landmark.Outskirts / Tuareg Camps: Traditional Tuareg encampments on the town's edge
hood_landmark.Airport Road District: Tamanrasset's newer residential and administrative quarter

avoid.reason: Avoid independent travel outside town — the desert border zones toward Mali, Niger and Libya carry kidnapping and terrorism risk, and excursions require authorized guides or escorts.
Register with local authorities, expect police checkpoints, and only visit the Ahaggar/Assekrem with a licensed guide.

hood_desc: The commercial core with the market, museum, and most hotels; the practical base before heading into the Hoggar.
A multi-day excursion base deep in the Hoggar mountains, reached only by 4x4, famous for its sunrise and sunset views.
A quiet hilltop area a short drive from town, home to the hermitage of Charles de Foucauld and sweeping desert views.
Semi-permanent Tuareg camps on the edge of town where visitors can experience traditional nomadic hospitality.
A newer, quieter residential district with government buildings and the road out to the airport.

water.note: Drink bottled or treated water only.

transit.sys: Local taxis and guide-arranged 4x4 vehicles; no formal bus network
transit.hours: Daylight hours; desert travel after dark is avoided
transit.pay: Cash to the driver or guide
transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels and tour agencies arrange transport
transit.note: A licensed desert guide is effectively required for any trip into the Hoggar mountains or Assekrem

transport.air: Tamanrasset Airport (TMR) with domestic flights from Algiers
transport.bus: Long-distance buses run along the Trans-Sahara Highway to Algiers (multi-day journey)
transport.car: The Trans-Sahara Highway connects Tamanrasset to northern Algeria; a guide is recommended for any off-highway desert travel

net.m: Moderate 3G/4G in town, no coverage in the deep desert
net.w: Wifi available in some hotels but often slow
net.gb: ~$5-10 for a prepaid tourist SIM (passport required to register)
net.fwn: Wifi available in central hotels, though unreliable
net.ap: A Mobilis or Djezzy prepaid SIM, registered with your passport

tip.s: 10% is customary and appreciated for desert guides
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory

food.name: Taguella
food.desc: Tuareg sand bread: a thick wheat disc buried under hot sand and embers, dusted off, torn into pieces and drowned in a spiced goat or camel meat sauce.

places.name: Tassili Restaurant
places.note: Town-centre kitchen serving Tuareg food, with taguella baked fresh and lamb sauces.

places.name: Hotel Tahat
places.note: The long-standing landmark hotel; its dining room does taguella for guests and groups.

places.name: Hoggar guide camps and Assekrem bivouacs
places.note: Trek crews bake taguella in the fire pit at night - the way it is meant to be eaten.

food.name: Saharan couscous
food.desc: Hand-rolled semolina steamed over a broth of goat, camel or dried meat with carrot, turnip and chickpeas; Friday lunch and the default guest dish.

places.name: Sahara Taste Restaurant
places.note: Known to locals and visitors alike for generous, heavily spiced Algerian plates.

places.name: Tassili Restaurant
places.note: Traditional menu covering both Tuareg and mainstream Algerian cooking.

places.name: Hotel Tahat
places.note: Reliable couscous in a town where full restaurants are few.

food.name: Grilled camel and goat
food.desc: Camel meat cut thin and grilled over charcoal, or goat slow-cooked mechoui-style until it falls apart, eaten with bread and harissa rather than cutlery.

places.name: Sahara Taste Restaurant
places.note: Spiced grilled meats are the house strength; portions are large.

places.name: Tamanrasset central market grills
places.note: Butchers with braziers grill what they have just cut; the cheapest hot meal in town.

places.name: Tassili Restaurant
places.note: Cooks the local meats in stews and grills in a rustic, low-key room.

food.name: Chorba and tomato-rich stews
food.desc: Thin soup of lamb, vermicelli, chickpeas and dried tomato scented with coriander and cinnamon - the standard opener, welcome after cold desert nights.

places.name: Tassili Restaurant
places.note: Chorba appears daily; a good, cheap opener before the meat course.

places.name: Sahara Taste Restaurant
places.note: Tagine-style stews and soups alongside the grills.

places.name: Hotel Tahat
places.note: Set menus usually open with chorba, especially in winter.

food.name: Mahdjouba
food.desc: Paper-thin semolina dough folded around a slow-cooked onion and tomato filling, then griddled - Algeria's great street snack, sold folded in paper.

places.name: Tamanrasset central market stalls
places.note: Griddle carts fold and fry mahdjouba to order through the afternoon.

places.name: Sahara Taste Restaurant
places.note: Offers the fried semolina breads alongside its main dishes.

places.name: Bakeries along Avenue Emir Abdelkader
places.note: Neighbourhood bakeries selling kesra, mahdjouba and sweet pastries.

food.name: Hoggar dates with camel milk
food.desc: Dates from the oasis gardens south of town, eaten with fresh or soured camel milk; pounded with millet and goat cheese they become the Tuareg drink eghajira.

places.name: Tamanrasset central market
places.note: Sacks of oasis dates by variety, plus dried cheese and millet for eghajira.

places.name: Abalessa and Tit oasis gardens
places.note: Palm gardens where growers sell dates direct at harvest time.

places.name: Hoggar guide camps
places.note: Dates and camel milk are the standard welcome offered to arriving guests.

food.name: Tuareg tea
food.desc: Green tea boiled with sugar and mint, poured from height into small glasses three times: bitter as death, sweet as life, gentle as love. Refusing is not done.

places.name: Hoggar guide camps and Assekrem bivouacs
places.note: The full three-glass ritual over a fire is the point of a night in the mountains.

places.name: Tamanrasset central market tea stalls
places.note: Men brew on tiny charcoal braziers beside the stalls all day; sit down and you will be poured one.

places.name: Tassili Restaurant
places.note: Serves the tea after meals for visitors who want the ritual without the desert.

food.name: Karkade hibiscus infusion
food.desc: Dried hibiscus flowers steeped into a deep red, tart drink, sweetened heavily and served hot or chilled; the standard non-alcoholic refresher of the Sahara.

places.name: Tamanrasset central market
places.note: Dried hibiscus sold loose by weight beside the spice and date stalls.

places.name: Sahara Taste Restaurant
places.note: Keeps karkade and mint infusions on the drinks list alongside the meals.

places.name: Cafes along Avenue Emir Abdelkader
places.note: Street cafes pour karkade, coffee and mint tea from morning to late evening.

landmarks: Assekrem Plateau
A windswept 2,700-metre plateau in the Hoggar whose name means 'the end of the world', delivering the Sahara's most spellbinding sunrise panorama.
Hermitage of Charles de Foucauld (Assekrem)
The stone refuge built in 1911 by the hermit-priest of the Sahara, still tended by monks atop the Assekrem plateau.
Ahaggar National Park
A vast protected wilderness of jagged volcanic peaks, lunar plains and Tuareg encampments surrounding Tamanrasset, among Earth's most otherworldly desert landscapes.
Mount Tahat
Algeria's highest summit at 2,908 metres, a stark volcanic horn rising from the Hoggar massif that challenges adventurous trekkers.
Pic Iharen
A dramatic granite-basalt monolith towering over the approach to Tamanrasset, the city's unmistakable natural landmark and a favourite photo stop.
Tomb of Tin Hinan (Abalessa)
The 4th-century stone tomb of the legendary Tuareg ancestral queen, excavated with golden jewellery, in an oasis 80 kilometres west of town.
Afilal Gueltas
Rare permanent rock pools high in the Hoggar where spring water, reeds and birdlife create a startling oasis amid black volcanic desert.
The Frigate (Charles de Foucauld's house in Tamanrasset)
The humble mud-brick 'bordj' where the French hermit lived and died in 1916, preserved as a small museum in the town centre.
Maison de l'Artisanat
Tamanrasset's craft centre, where Tuareg silversmiths sell the famous Cross of Agadez, leatherwork and indigo cloth beneath tamarisk-shaded arcades.
Tit Village
A historic oasis village near Tamanrasset, site of the 1902 battle that ended Tuareg resistance to French rule, with traditional red-earth architecture.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in southern Algeria - SNTF's network (https://www.sntf.dz/) is confined to the north. Tamanrasset is about 2,000 km from Algiers by road. Most visitors fly into Tamanrasset airport; the overland route is a two-day desert drive.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches - the borders with Niger and Mali have been closed or unsafe for years, so the old Trans-Saharan route through In Guezzam is not a practical option. Check your government's travel advisory before considering it. SNTV coaches run north to Ghardaïa and Algiers, taking two days with an overnight stop. Buy at the terminal in cash.

ferry.note: Tamanrasset sits at 1,400 m in the Hoggar mountains in the central Sahara, about as far from navigable water as it is possible to be, so there are no ferries.

full.name: Tazrouk
full.blurb: Small Tuareg village at the base of the Atakor massif, used as a stop en route into the Ahaggar mountains.

full.name: Silet
full.blurb: Small desert town along the Trans-Sahara Highway south of Tamanrasset, near a seasonal riverbed.
